competencies.title: Can name and talk about feelings
Can take turns and share in a group
Can solve a disagreement calmly and fairly
Can listen carefully and repeat back what was said
Can name community helpers and how they help
Can explain some rights every child has
Can compare how different governments work
Can explain how a vote and a new law work
Can check if a news story or post is reliable
Can compare everyday life in two societies

items.subject: feelings
items.title: Feelings faces
items.summary: Faces can show how we feel. Let's make some!
steps: 😊 Make a happy face.
😢 Make a sad face.
😠 Make a cross face.
😨 Make a scared face.
🗣️ Say: "I feel happy when..."
🤗 Big feelings are OK. We can tell a grown-up.

check.question: This face 😢 feels...
check.explain: Yes, tears can mean sad. It is OK to feel sad.

items.adultNote: Use a mirror if you have one. Name feelings during the day too ("You look proud!"). All feelings are allowed; some actions are not.

items.subject: kindness and cooperation
items.title: Roll the ball, take a turn
items.summary: Taking turns makes games fun for everyone.
steps: 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Sit in a circle.
⚽ Roll the ball to someone.
🗣️ Say their name.
⏳ Wait for the ball to come back.
👏 Clap for good waiting!

safety.notes: Use a soft ball and a clear floor space.

basic.description: Roll a sock ball between family members.

better.description: Use a soft ball and add a turn-taking song.

advanced.description: Use a sand timer so each person gets an equal turn.

substitutions.use: Rolled-up socks or a scrunched paper ball

items.adultNote: With one child, play with an adult or a toy that "takes a turn". Praise waiting, not winning.

items.subject: community helpers
items.title: Who helps us?
items.summary: Lots of people help our community every day.
steps: 🚒 Firefighters put out fires.
🧑‍⚕️ Doctors and nurses help sick people.
👮 Police officers help keep people safe.
🧑‍🌾 Farmers grow our food.
🧹 Cleaners keep places tidy.
👋 Who helps you? Draw them!

check.question: Who puts out fires?
check.explain: Yes! Firefighters put out fires and rescue people.

items.adultNote: Mention that anyone can do any of these jobs. Teach how to get help where you live (see the emergency numbers screen).

items.subject: friendship
items.title: What makes a good friend?
items.summary: Good friends are kind, fair and listen to each other.
steps: Think of a time a friend was kind to you.
Good friends share, take turns and say sorry.
Good friends do not make you keep secrets that feel bad.
You can be a good friend too.
Draw a "friend recipe": what goes into a good friend?

check.question: A friend takes your toy without asking. What can you say?
check.explain: Saying how you feel, calmly, helps friends understand.

check.question: Should a friend ask you to keep a secret that makes you feel bad?
check.explain: No. Tell a trusted adult about any secret that worries you.

items.adultNote: Children who are home-educated may have fewer peers; siblings, cousins and neighbours count as friends.

items.subject: rules and fairness
items.title: Make fair family rules
items.summary: Rules help groups get along. Fair rules work for everyone.
steps: Talk about a rule you already have at home.
Ask: who does this rule help?
Think of a new rule together, for example about tidying up.
Check it is fair: does it work for everyone?
Write or draw the rule and put it on the wall.
After a week, talk about whether it worked.

check.question: A fair rule...
options: works for everyone in the group
check.explain: Fair rules think about everyone they affect.

items.adultNote: Let the child genuinely change at least one small rule. This is a first taste of how rules and laws are made.

items.subject: conflict resolution
items.title: Only one swing
items.summary: Two children want the same swing. What can you do?
steps: Read the story.
Choose what to do at each step.
Talk about your choices with a grown-up.

safety.notes: A talking game. No physical activity.

simulation.scenario: You and another child both run to the only swing at the same time. You both feel cross.

options.text: Take a deep breath to calm down
options.feedback: Yes. Calm bodies help us think.
Pushing can hurt someone. Let's find a better way.

options.text: "Can we take turns? You go, then me."
options.feedback: Great idea. Taking turns is fair.
That might start an argument. Try asking to share.

steps.prompt: The other child will not take turns. What now?

options.feedback: Good choice. Adults can help when we are stuck.
Shouting rarely helps. A grown-up can help.

items.subject: communication
items.title: Say it with "I feel..."
items.summary: "I feel" sentences help people understand you without starting a fight.
steps: Learn the pattern: "I feel ___ when ___ because ___. Could we ___?"
Example: "I feel upset when you use my pens without asking, because they break. Could you ask first?"
Practise turning three "You always..." sentences into "I feel..." sentences.
Now practise listening: your partner says one, you repeat it back in your own words.
Swap roles.

check.question: Which one is an "I feel" sentence?
check.explain: Yes. It says how you feel without blaming.

items.subject: rights and responsibilities
items.title: Rights every child has
items.summary: Nearly every country in the world has agreed that children have special rights.
steps: In 1989 the United Nations agreed the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
It says every child has rights, wherever they live.
Some rights: to be safe, to learn, to play, to have healthy food and care, to have a name, and to be listened to.
Rights belong to every child equally, whatever their gender, religion, language or ability.
Rights come with respect: my rights matter, and so do other people's.
Pick three rights and draw what each looks like in real life.

sources.title: Convention on the Rights of the Child

check.question: Who do children's rights belong to?
Which of these is a right in the Convention?
check.explain: Play and rest are rights. A phone is nice to have, but it is not a right.

items.adultNote: If anything here worries the child about their own safety, listen calmly and seek help from local child-protection services.

items.subject: rights and responsibilities
items.title: Rights and responsibilities pairs
items.summary: With each right comes a way we can respect other people's rights.
steps: Write five rights on cards, for example "the right to learn".
For each one, write a matching responsibility, for example "let others learn too".
Mix the cards up and match them again.
Talk: who else has responsibilities to make sure children's rights happen? (parents, governments)

sources.title: Convention on the Rights of the Child

items.adultNote: Make clear that rights are not "earned" by good behaviour: children have them anyway.

items.subject: government
items.title: How are countries run?
items.summary: Countries are run in different ways. Let's compare how decisions are made.
steps: Every government needs ways to make laws, carry them out and settle disputes.
In a representative democracy, people vote for representatives. Some have a president chosen separately (presidential); others have a prime minister chosen from parliament (parliamentary).
In a direct democracy, people vote on some decisions themselves, for example in a referendum.
In a constitutional monarchy, a king or queen is head of state, but elected leaders make most decisions.
In an absolute monarchy, the monarch holds most power.
In a one-party state, one political party leads the government and other parties cannot compete for power.
Many countries mix features. Make a table: who makes laws, how leaders are chosen, how leaders can be changed.
Pick two countries and fill in the table using an atlas or a reliable encyclopedia.

check.question: In a parliamentary system, the prime minister usually...
options: is chosen by the monarch alone
check.explain: Yes. In most parliamentary systems the leader needs the support of parliament.

check.question: A referendum is when...
options: people vote directly on a question
check.explain: Right. It is a form of direct democracy.

items.adultNote: Keep this descriptive and comparative. Avoid telling the child which party or leader to support; encourage questions about how each system protects people and handles disagreement.

items.subject: voting
items.title: Hold a family vote
items.summary: Different ways of counting votes can give different results. Try it!
steps: Choose a real family decision, for example which dinner to cook on Friday, with 3-4 options.
Vote 1: everyone picks one favourite. The most votes wins ("first past the post").
Vote 2: everyone ranks the options 1, 2, 3. Remove the last place and move those votes to their next choice until one option has more than half ("ranked choice").
Compare: did the same option win both times?
Learn: many countries use proportional representation, where seats match the share of votes.
Discuss: why do people vote in secret? Why does every vote count the same?

check.question: Why is voting often secret?
options: So people can choose freely without pressure
check.explain: Secret ballots protect people from pressure or fear.

items.subject: laws
items.title: How does a law get made?
items.summary: Laws are rules for a whole country. Most go through several steps before they apply.
steps: Laws protect people, settle disagreements and organise shared services.
In many countries: an idea is written as a draft law (a bill).
Lawmakers debate it and may change it.
They vote. Some countries need two chambers or a head of state to agree.
Courts can decide what a law means and whether it follows the constitution.
Find out how laws are made in your country. Draw it as a flow chart.
Compare with one other country.

check.question: What is a bill?
options: A finished law that cannot change
check.explain: Yes, a bill is a proposed law.

items.subject: media literacy
items.title: Check before you share
items.summary: Not everything online or in the news is true. Learn four quick checks.
steps: Stop: notice how the post makes you feel. Strong feelings are a sign to slow down.
Source: who made this? Are they known and accountable?
Search: do other trusted sources report the same thing?
Trace: find the original photo, quote or study.
Practise on three headlines an adult picks for you, from paper or screen.
Score each one: reliable, unsure or misleading, and explain why.

check.question: A post makes you very angry. What should you do first?
check.explain: Strong emotions are a reason to check before sharing.

check.question: An advert and a news report are...
options: different: one wants to sell you something
check.explain: Ask what each one wants you to do or think.

items.adultNote: Choose examples from a range of outlets and viewpoints so the lesson is about checking methods, not about which side is right.

items.subject: debate
items.title: Hold a fair debate
items.summary: A good debater can explain the other side so well that the other side agrees it is fair.
steps: Pick a question with reasonable views on more than one side, for example "Should our town add more bike lanes?"
Research both sides using at least three different sources.
Write the strongest case FOR and the strongest case AGAINST.
Debate with a family member: 3 minutes each, then 2 minutes to reply.
Rules: no insults, quote fairly, admit good points.
Swap sides and debate again.
Reflect: what did you learn from the side you disagreed with?

safety.notes: A discussion project. Keep it respectful and stop if it becomes upsetting.

basic.description: Debate with one family member at home.

better.description: Use cards for key points and time each speech.

advanced.description: Record the debate, watch it back and score clarity, evidence and fairness.

substitutions.use: Count slowly or use a kitchen clock
Write both sides yourself and read them aloud

items.adultNote: Avoid topics that are painful for the family. For politically charged topics, judge the reasoning, not the conclusion.

items.subject: comparative societies
items.title: Two societies, side by side
items.summary: Compare everyday life in your country and one other country.
steps: Pick a country you know little about.
Research: how is it governed? What languages are spoken? What do children do at school and at home?
Find: main work and industries, food, festivals and how people travel.
Make a side-by-side chart with your own country.
Note what is similar as well as what is different.
Write one paragraph on something you admire there and one question you still have.
Avoid stereotypes: one country contains many different people.

safety.notes: A research project. Use sources an adult agrees on.

basic.description: Research from library books and draw a chart.

better.description: Make a poster with a map of both countries.

advanced.description: Make a short slideshow or video presentation.

substitutions.use: A free online map on a phone

items.adultNote: If the family has a study language, choose a country where it is spoken.

items.subject: community
items.title: Make something better nearby
items.summary: Spot a small problem in your community and plan a helpful, safe way to improve it.
steps: List small problems you notice: litter, a lonely neighbour, no book swap.
Pick one you can actually help with.
Ask: who already works on this? Could you help them?
Make a plan: steps, people, cost, time and risks.
Get adult approval, then try it.
Measure the result and tell people what happened.

hazards: Litter can be sharp or dirty
safety.notes: An adult agrees the plan, knows where you are and joins for anything outside the home. Wear gloves and use a picker for litter; never touch needles or broken glass.

basic.description: Help a neighbour or family member with something they need.

better.description: Organise a small litter pick with family.

advanced.description: Set up a book or seed swap with adult permission from the place owner.
